newsitem.title: INDIA: India truck owners return to work after strike.
newsitem.headline: India truck owners return to work after strike.

text.p: Indian truck owners returned to work on Thursday after a 10-day strike that crippled industry and pushed up prices but they said freight rates would rise before the situation returned to normal in two weeks' time.
"It will take 15 days for goods piled up to be cleared," S.P. Singh, spokesman of the All-India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), told Reuters.
"The freight rate will go up by 15 to 20 percent during this period. There will be less trucks chasing more goods. The rates will normalise after that," another AIMTC official added.

Truck owners on Wednesday ended the strike after the government agreed to their demand that they not be responsible for collecting a five percent service tax and to hold a proposed rise in insurance premiums in abeyance.
The AIMTC, which represents nearly 2.2 million truck owners, said the strike had been called off in all states expect the western state of Maharashtra.
"The strike is over except in Maharashtra," Singh said. "The problem will be in the western sector where in Maharashtra the strike still continues. They have some local demand."

Spokesman Dayanand Natkar of the Maharashtra Rajya Truck Tempo Tankers Bus Mahasangh, which represents 180 associations with about 200,000 members in the western state, said they wanted to scrap an increase in local motor vehicle and sales taxes, along with other demands.
Maharashtra is India's commercial centre, and its capital, Bombay, is the country's busiest port.
Singh said the truck owners in Maharashtra are scheduled to have a meeting with the state government on Thursday.
"Hopefully the strike in Bombay will end by today night," R.D. Joshi, manager of Bombay Port Trust, told Reuters.
Singh said truck owners had lost about 36 billion rupees ($1 billion) due to the strike. Analysts said the economy faced an estimated loss of about 70 to 80 billion rupees ($1.9 billion) per day.
"By today evening about 450,000 trucks will be on the roads," Singh said. It would be two to three days before all trucks took to the roads as most drivers had gone on leave.

"Fruit and vegetable prices have gone up by at least 25 percent in different states," said an official of the Punjab, Haryana and Delhi Chambers of Commerce and Industry (PHDCCI). "But it will normalise soon."
The PHDCCI official said industrial production in the northern states had come to a "grinding halt" and estimated it would take two days before it restarted.
"We are still working out the loss (faced by the industry)," he said.
Analysts said the arrivals at market of summer rice, wheat and oilseed crops had come to a standstill.
Shipping had also been hit. "I expect a lot of export commitments to be cancelled," said one Bombay-based commodity analyst. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
